title: Carboxylic Acids
path: Structure and Properties of Alcohols, Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids and Amines

headings.title: Introduction to Carboxylic Acids and the Carboxyl Functional Group
headings.content: Carboxylic acids are organic compounds containing the **carboxyl group**, which is a combination of a carbonyl group (C=O) and a hydroxyl group (-OH) attached to the same carbon atom. The general formula is written as R-COOH. In this arrangement, the carbon-oxygen double bond and the single-bonded hydroxyl oxygen pull electron density away from the central carbon and the acidic hydrogen. This specific electronic layout gives the class of molecules their distinct chemical behavior, notably their ability to donate a proton in aqueous solutions.

headings.title: Nomenclature and Structural Classification
headings.content: Naming carboxylic acids involves replacing the 'e' ending of the corresponding alkane with **-oic acid**. The carbon of the carboxyl group is always assigned position number one in IUPAC nomenclature. For example, a one-carbon acid is methanoic acid (commonly known as formic acid), while a two-carbon chain is ethanoic acid (acetic acid). Many simple carboxylic acids also retain their historical common names derived from natural sources, such as butyric acid from butter.

headings.title: Physical Properties: Boiling Points and Solubility in Aqueous Systems
headings.content: Carboxylic acids have remarkably high boiling points compared to alkanes, alcohols, or aldehydes of similar molecular weight. This occurs because two carboxylic acid molecules can form two hydrogen bonds simultaneously, creating a stable **dimer**. Regarding solubility, smaller carboxylic acids mix completely with water due to hydrogen bonding between the water molecules and the polar carboxyl group. However, as the non-polar hydrocarbon tail grows longer past five carbons, water solubility drops sharply.

headings.title: Acidity and Resonance Stabilization of the Carboxylate Ion
headings.content: Carboxylic acids are weak acids that dissociate in water to yield a proton and a **carboxylate ion**. Unlike simple alcohols, the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid benefits immensely from **resonance stabilization**. The negative charge is delocalized equally across both oxygen atoms through the pi bond system. This sharing lowers the overall energy of the ion, making the parent molecule much more willing to give up its hydrogen ion.

headings.title: Key Chemical Reactions: Esterification, Salt Formation, and Reduction
headings.content:
Carboxylic acids participate in several fundamental organic reactions:
- **Esterification**: Reacting a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst produces an ester and water.
- **Salt Formation**: Neutralizing a carboxylic acid with a strong base like sodium hydroxide yields a water-soluble carboxylate salt and water.
- **Reduction**: Strong reducing agents like lithium aluminum hydride convert carboxylic acids directly into primary alcohols.

headings.title: Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Significance in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Carboxylic acid structures appear frequently in pharmacology and biochemistry. For instance, **acetylsalicylic acid** (aspirin) contains both an aromatic carboxylic acid component and an ester group, acting as an analgesic and anti-inflammatory agent. Additionally, fatty acids are long-chain carboxylic acids vital for cellular structure and energy storage in the human body. Understanding these structures helps healthcare providers comprehend drug solubility, metabolic pathways, and acid-base balance in clinical settings.
